Dan Patrick's Election Loss Reopens Texas Gambling Debate

Published November 11, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Texas remains one of the largest states without legal sports betting or commercial casinos, and the biggest reason why has long been a single office: the lieutenant governor, who controls which bills the state Senate ever votes on. That changed on November 3, when Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick lost his reelection bid to Democrat Vikki Goodwin, a state representative who has supported letting Texans vote on expanded gambling.

What actually flipped in the election

Patrick's defeat was part of a broader Democratic sweep at the top of the Texas ballot: Democrat Gina Hinojosa also defeated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, and Democrats won control of the Texas House. Republicans held onto their Senate majority, with 19 Republican seats to 12 Democratic seats, according to local coverage of the results from Houston's KPRC/Click2Houston. That Senate math matters because any sports betting or casino measure in Texas has to pass as a constitutional amendment, not an ordinary bill — requiring two-thirds approval in both the House and Senate before it even goes to voters.

Why Patrick's seat specifically mattered

As lieutenant governor, Patrick controlled the Texas Senate's calendar and had been the chamber's most consistent roadblock to gambling expansion, according to both KPRC and Casinos.com's reporting on the race. In 2023, the Texas House passed a sports betting constitutional amendment by a wide 101-42 margin, but the Senate never brought it to a vote under Patrick's leadership. Casinos.com also reported that a second push during the 2025 session failed after three lawmakers who had supported the 2023 amendment switched sides.

Goodwin's win removes that specific gatekeeper, which both outlets frame as a real but incomplete change: KPRC's reporting notes the shift "removes a major obstacle that has prevented gambling legislation from advancing through the Texas Senate," while stressing that any amendment would still need two-thirds support from a Senate where Republicans retain the majority.

The math that still has to work out

Clearing a Texas constitutional amendment requires at least 100 of 150 House votes and 21 of 31 Senate votes, then a simple majority of statewide voters. The next regular legislative session begins January 12, 2027, with most bills due by mid-March, according to Casinos.com. Casinos.com reports the earliest realistic statewide vote on such an amendment would be November 2027, with legal sportsbooks potentially live in 2028 on an accelerated timeline and commercial casinos likely taking longer given additional licensing and siting requirements.

Governor-elect Hinojosa's own record complicates a simple reading of the results: as a state representative in 2023, she voted against the gambling package that included sports betting and destination-resort casinos, and neither outlet reports her announcing a new position since winning. The governor has no veto power over a constitutional amendment, but her stance could still shape how hard the new administration pushes the issue.

Why it matters for bettors: nothing about Texas law has changed yet, and both outlets are clear on that point. What changed is that the single biggest procedural blocker to a Senate vote is gone, and public support is already substantial — a 2025 University of Houston poll cited by Casinos.com found 60% of Texans backed legal sports betting. Whether that translates into an actual amendment reaching voters now depends on the 2027 legislative session, not the election itself.
